title: The Atlas's own inherent authority is a provenance type, so some Executive actions need no fresh vote
content:
A.1.10.2.4.5.1.4 defines strong document type provenance as "actions approved by Sky Governance either directly (as through a Governance Poll) **or through the inherent authority of the Sky Atlas**." Such provenance is "very hard to modify, as [it] cannot be modified or changed without a subsequent vote," is "always public in nature," and carries "practically no account compromise risk with this category of provenance as all changes go through a vote and review process."

The two sources in that definition work differently in time. A Governance Poll is a fresh, specific authorization for one action. The Atlas is a standing authorization: because a provision was voted into the Atlas once, actions it mandates are already approved and need no new vote each cycle.

That is what makes recurring Executive content possible at all. Routine operations execute weekly on the authority of text ratified long ago, and the vote-cost is paid once when the rule is written rather than every time it is applied.

It also explains why the Atlas is so specific about parameters and procedures elsewhere. If the Atlas is itself the authorization, then vagueness in the Atlas is vagueness in the mandate — a loosely worded provision grants broader standing authority than any single poll ever would. Precision in the document is a limit on discretion, not pedantry.
description: A.1.10.2.4.5.1.4 puts Governance Poll approval and 'the inherent authority of the Sky Atlas' in one category, making the Atlas a standing authorization whose only edit path is another vote.
